q1_eu_ai_act.product_context: Consumer photo-library person-tagging / face-clustering on user-uploaded photos (not public-space surveillance; not law enforcement). Inference on remote SaaS backend.

a_risk_class.summary: Not an Art.5 prohibition if you do not scrape the open internet/CCTV to build FR DBs, do not do real-time RBI in public spaces for LE, and do not categorise by race/politics/religion/sexual orientation etc. High-risk Annex III biometrics may still be in play for 'remote biometric identification' (1a); pure person-clustering without sensitive-attribute inference is outside Annex III 1b/1c. Classification for private-library tagging is contested—document an Art.6 assessment.

evidence.claim: Art.5(1)(e) prohibits AI that creates/expands facial recognition databases via untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV—out of scope for user-uploaded own-library processing.

Art.5(1)(g) prohibits biometric categorisation systems that deduce race, political opinions, trade union membership, religion/beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation from biometrics (with narrow LE/labelling exceptions)—not mere 'Person A / Person B' identity clustering.
Art.5(1)(h) prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement (with limited exceptions)—not applicable to private photo-library SaaS.

Annex III point 1 high-risk biometrics (where permitted under Union/national law): (a) remote biometric identification systems (excluding verification whose sole purpose is confirm-claimant-is-who-they-claim); (b) biometric categorisation according to sensitive/protected attributes inferred from biometrics; (c) emotion recognition.

Art.3 defines 'remote biometric identification system' as AI identifying natural persons without their active involvement, typically at a distance, by comparing a person's biometric data with biometric data in a reference database; 'biometric categorisation system' assigns persons to categories on biometric data unless ancillary to another commercial service and strictly necessary for objective technical reasons.

Commission AI Act Service Desk biometrics guidance lists 'facial/voice recognition for media archives' (identify selected individuals from audiovisual content against a reference database without active involvement) as in-scope for Annex III 1(a) RBI—closest official analogy to photo tagging against a gallery.

Same Commission guidance: biometric categorisation high-risk only where assigning sensitive/protected attributes (Art.9 GDPR style); age/gender categorisation examples are often out of 1(b). Person-label clusters without sensitive inference are not 1(b).

Whether a closed, account-holder-only face gallery (Google/Apple Photos style) is 'RBI high-risk' remains unsettled; conservative reading treats 1:N matching of templates from third-party faces in user libraries as potential RBI; provider should document Art.6 classification (and any Art.6(3) non-high-risk argument) before market placement.

If classified high-risk Annex III, provider obligations include risk management, data governance, technical documentation, transparency to deployers, human oversight, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity, conformity assessment, CE marking, and registration (Arts.8–16, 43, 47–49, Annex IV).

b_obligations_timeline.summary: Phased. After Digital Omnibus on AI, EC Service Desk: Annex III high-risk rules apply 2 Dec 2027 (not original 2 Aug 2026). GPAI Chapter V already from 2 Aug 2025. Prohibitions from 2 Feb 2025. Art.50 transparency from 2 Aug 2026.

evidence.claim: Official EC AI Act Service Desk timeline (post-Digital Omnibus): 1 Aug 2024 entry into force; 2 Feb 2025 prohibitions + general provisions/AI literacy; 2 Aug 2025 GPAI rules + governance; 2 Aug 2026 majority of rules + Art.50 transparency + enforcement of GPAI/prohibitions/transparency; 2 Dec 2027 Annex III high-risk rules; 2 Aug 2028 Annex I product-embedded high-risk.

Digital Omnibus provisional political agreement deferred standalone Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I product-embedded high-risk to 2 August 2028 (from original Aug 2026 / Aug 2027).
GPAI model provider obligations (Art.53 et seq.) apply from 2 August 2025; models placed on the market before that date must comply by 2 August 2027 (Art.111 transitional).
Art.50 transparency obligations start applying 2 August 2026 per EC Service Desk.

c_gpai_vs_task_specific.summary: Task-specific face-recognition / embedding models are generally NOT GPAI. Art.53 training-content public summary binds providers of general-purpose AI models only.

evidence.claim: Art.3(63): GPAI model = model trained with large data using self-supervision at scale that displays significant generality and can competently perform a wide range of distinct tasks, integrable into various downstream systems.
Recital 98: models with ≥1B parameters trained with large self-supervised data should be considered to display significant generality; Recital 99: large generative models are typical GPAI examples.
Commission Q&A indicative criterion: training compute >10^23 FLOP and ability to generate language / text-to-image / text-to-video for GPAI classification guidance.

Art.53(1)(d) obliges GPAI providers to draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of training content per AI Office template—this obligation is for general-purpose AI models, not ordinary narrow AI systems.

A proprietary in-house face-embedding model used only for person matching in photo libraries is a narrow/task-specific AI system/model and should not, on ordinary reading of Art.3(63), trigger GPAI Chapter V (including the training-data summary template).

d_provider_disclose_vs_document.summary: If non-high-risk: limited AI Act transparency (Art.50 if any emotion/biometric interaction labels apply); GDPR transparency dominates. If high-risk Annex III: heavy internal Annex IV tech docs + deployer info Art.13 + EU database registration Art.49/71; public CE/conformity. GPAI public training summary only if model is GPAI.

evidence.claim: High-risk providers must draw up technical documentation before placing on market (Art.11 + Annex IV content: system description, design specs, data governance, risk management, metrics, human oversight, cybersecurity, etc.)—primarily internal / authority-facing, not a public dump.

Art.13 requires high-risk providers to design systems so deployers can interpret outputs and use them appropriately, and to provide instructions for use including characteristics, performance, limitations, human oversight measures.
Art.49 + Chapter VIII / Art.71: high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III must be registered in the EU database before placing on the market (provider registration duties).
Art.53 GPAI public training-content summary and technical docs for authorities/downstream apply only to GPAI model providers, not to ordinary face models.

No Commission guidance found that expressly carves consumer photo-tagging apps out of Annex III 1(a); closest official material is Service Desk RBI/media-archive examples—classification must be product-specific legal analysis.

q2_gdpr.summary: Face templates/embeddings used to uniquely identify persons are Art.9 special-category biometric data. Default ban; explicit consent (Art.9(2)(a)) is the realistic basis for consumer SaaS. DPIA almost always required. Privacy policy must cover biometric processing purpose, legal bases, retention, recipients (backend), rights, international transfers.

evidence.claim: Art.9(1) GDPR prohibits processing of 'biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person' unless an Art.9(2) exception applies; Art.9(2)(a) is explicit consent.

Art.4(14) defines biometric data as personal data from specific technical processing of physical/physiological/behavioural characteristics that allow or confirm unique identification (e.g. facial images, fingerprints).

Recital 51: photographs are not systematically special category; they become biometric special-category data only when processed through specific technical means allowing unique identification/authentication—i.e. face templates/embeddings for matching cross that line.

ICO: digital photos are not automatically biometric; they become biometric special category when you create digital templates used for automated matching/identification; DPIA required for special category on large scale / biometric in combination with other high-risk criteria.

EDPB Guidelines 3/2019 (video devices): raw video is not itself Art.9 biometric data until specific technical processing for unique identification; three criteria (nature, means of technical processing, purpose of unique ID) apply.

Comparable consumer FR: Facebook disabled Tag Suggest / facial recognition in EU after DPA pressure (2012 templates deletion); Meta later globally shut Face Recognition (2021) and deleted >1B facial templates—illustrates regulatory/commercial risk of FR templates.

Clearview AI fined €30.5M by Dutch DPA (2024) for illegal collection of face images for FR; multiple EU DPAs (FR, GR, IT, NL) have sanctioned Clearview (~€100M cumulative reported)—scraped internet FR is the polar opposite of consented private libraries but shows Art.9/lawfulness enforcement intensity.

Legal basis used by comparable products: for consumer FR/tagging in EU, industry and DPA practice converge on explicit consent from data subjects; legitimate interest is generally unavailable for Art.9 biometrics.

Hard problem for photo libraries: account-holder consent does not substitute for consent of third-party photo subjects (family, guests) whose faces become templates—GDPR requires data-subject consent for special category processing of those persons.

Privacy policy / Art.13–14 notice should state: biometric processing for person tagging; Art.6 + Art.9 legal bases; categories (photos, embeddings, labels); recipients (SaaS processor/controller, subprocessors); retention/deletion of templates; rights (access, erasure, withdraw consent); transfers; DPIA existence if required; no automated decisions with legal effects if none.

q3_us_bipa.summary: Illinois BIPA §15 requires notice + written release from the SUBJECT of the biometric identifier before collecting face geometry scans. Account-holder-only consent is insufficient when third parties appear in photos—Facebook Tag Suggestions / Google Photos settlements turned on exactly that. Texas CUBI similar commercial-purpose consent (AG only). Washington RCW 19.375 narrower; excludes photos/data generated therefrom under that statute.

evidence.claim: BIPA defines biometric identifier to include 'scan of hand or face geometry' (photographs themselves excluded, but scans derived from photos are the classic litigated theory).

BIPA §15(b): before collecting/capturing biometric identifier/information, private entity must (1) inform subject in writing of collection/storage; (2) inform of purpose and retention term; (3) receive written release from the subject or legally authorized representative.

BIPA §15(a) public retention/destruction policy; §15(c) ban on selling/profiting from biometrics; §15(d) disclosure limits; §20 private right of action ($1k negligent / $5k intentional-or-reckless per violation, plus fees)—2024 amendments cap recovery for same method/person collection as single violation.
Facebook Tag Suggestions BIPA class settlement ≈ $650M (final approval 2021)—alleged face templates from uploaded photos without prior informed written consent of Illinois users.
Google Photos face-grouping BIPA settlement ≈ $100M (2022)—alleged creation of face templates without consent.
Meta/Instagram later BIPA settlement ≈ $68.5M (2023) reported in secondary sources.

Texas CUBI (Bus. & Com. Code ch. 503): for commercial purpose, may not capture biometric identifiers (incl. record of face geometry) without informing the individual and obtaining consent; restricts sale/disclosure; AG enforcement (no private right of action like BIPA); civil penalties up to $25k/violation reported in secondary charts.

Washington RCW 19.375: notice/consent (or opt-out mechanism) before enrolling biometric identifier for commercial purpose; definition excludes physical/digital photograph, video/audio or data generated therefrom—significantly narrower for photo-library face geometry vs BIPA/CUBI.

Templates from a user's own library still require §15 consent from PHOTO SUBJECTS (not merely account holder) under BIPA text: written release must be executed by 'the subject of the biometric identifier'—Facebook/Google settlements operationalize that reading for people depicted in photos.

Practical SaaS implication: pure account-holder ToS clickwrap is weak for multi-person libraries; risk mitigations discussed in industry commentary include opt-in per face, subject invitation/consent flows, IL geo-blocking of FR, or on-device processing with subject control—product/legal design choice, not settled statute text.

q4_wporg.summary: Freemium SaaS is allowed if the service is real and documented; trialware/crippleware of local code is banned. External calls need user consent + privacy documentation in readme. GPL for all code hosted on wp.org; remote paid SaaS backend need not be GPL.

evidence.claim: Guideline 1: Plugins must be GPL-compatible; all code, data, images in the wp.org plugin directory must be GPL or GPL-compatible; GPLv2-or-later strongly recommended.

Guideline 5 Trialware not permitted: may not lock functionality behind payment/upgrade, time/quota disable, or sandbox-only APIs. Paid service functionality IS permitted if all code inside the plugin is fully available; recommend external add-ons for premium code.

Guideline 6 SaaS permitted: plugins may interface to external third-party (incl. paid) services; service must provide substance and be clearly documented in the readme, preferably with Terms of Use link. Forbidden: license-key-only services when all function is local; sham services that only move code off-plugin; pure storefronts.

Guideline 7: Plugins may not contact external servers without explicit authorized consent (opt-in registration/checkbox). Documentation of how user data is collected/used in readme, preferably with privacy policy. SaaS exception: installing/activating/registering/configuring a documented service grants consent for those systems.
Guideline 8: may not send executable code via third-party systems; no remote plugin/theme installs; non-service JS/CSS must be local (fonts exception).
Guideline 9: implying users must pay to unlock included features is dishonest/prohibited; upselling ad-hoc products is acceptable within Guideline 11 (no admin hijacking).

Freemium norm: free wp.org client that honestly needs remote AI SaaS for alt-text/person tagging is allowed under G6; do not ship full local inference then key-gate it (G5 crippleware). Disclose remote processing, data sent, privacy policy in readme (G6+G7).

GPL scope: only what is distributed via wp.org must be GPL-compatible; proprietary remote backend weights/code hosted off-directory are normal for SaaS plugins—so long as the plugin interface is GPL and not a sham.

models.name: SAM 2
models.license: Apache-2.0 for code and model weights; SA-V dataset CC BY 4.0; eval code noted BSD-3 in Meta blog

models.name: PP-PicoDet
models.license: Apache-2.0 (PaddleDetection repository license; PicoDet is a PaddleDetection model family)
models.note: Repo-level Apache-2.0; confirm any specific pretrained weight notice in model zoo cards before shipping.

evidence.claim: Ultralytics docs: MobileSAM ~12 ms/image vs original SAM ~456 ms (same pipeline, Tiny-ViT 5M vs ViT-H 637M); MobileSAM ~5× smaller and ~7× faster than original SAM in published claims.

Ultralytics SAM-2 model table reports Meta SAM-b CPU latency on order of ~41,703 ms/image in their comparison table (desktop-class CPU figures—orders of magnitude too slow for interactive on-device ARM without quantization/specialized engines).
MobileSAM authors state the model can run relatively smoothly on CPU; project Apache-2.0.

PP-PicoDet paper: PicoDet-S reaches ~123–150 FPS on mobile ARM CPU (Snapdragon 865, input 320) with NCNN/Paddle Lite—detection, not SAM segmentation, but shows mobile ARM feasibility for light detectors.

Practical implication for ARM: full SAM2 is GPU/edge-NPU class; MobileSAM/EfficientSAM-class models are the realistic CPU/edge path; remote backend inference remains the reliable SaaS default for quality SAM-class masks.

q6_distillation.summary: No settled case law that NC model licenses automatically 'reach' pure outputs. Contract/license text of the NC model + ToS of commercial APIs control. InsightFace: code MIT; buffalo-class weights NC/research-only unless commercial pack licensed. OpenAI ToS expressly forbids using Output to develop competing models. Treat distillation from NC FR weights as high legal risk; train on synthetic/consented data or buy commercial licenses.

evidence.claim: InsightFace official README: code MIT (academic+commercial OK); training data with annotation and models trained with that data are non-commercial research only; both manual and auto-downloaded models follow NC research policy; contact recognition-oss-pack@insightface.ai for buffalo_l etc. commercial licensing.

InsightFace commercial site sells commercial usage rights for open-source model packages including buffalo_l, buffalo_s/m, antelopev2—implying default open weights are not free for commercial product use.

Whether an NC license on weights reaches embeddings/pseudo-labels/distilled student models is not clearly answered by InsightFace public license text; industry commentary treats using NC weights in any commercial pipeline (incl. distillation teachers) as non-compliant unless licensed—opinion, not adjudicated.
OpenAI Terms of Use: 'You may not … Use Output to develop models that compete with OpenAI'—contractual ban on competitive distillation from service outputs (not copyright statute).

Industry analyses of OpenAI–DeepSeek and similar disputes treat anti-distillation ToS clauses as the primary lever; enforceability of form ToS and proof of distillation remain contested (legal opinion).

Stanford Alpaca / self-instruct lineage: academic project using LLaMA (then non-commercial Meta license) + OpenAI-generated instruction data; widely discussed as ToS/license-risk precedent for commercial products, not a court holding that distillation is legal or illegal.

EU AI Act angle: Art.53(1)(c) GPAI copyright policy and training-content summary do not create a free right to train on third-party model outputs; copyright in model-generated data is unsettled under EU law; if training data includes personal data (face images), GDPR Art.9 still applies regardless of license laundering theories.

Commercial FR vendors: InsightFace sells OSS-model commercial packs and closed high-accuracy models—evidence that commercial licensing exists and is the intended path for product use of their FR weights. Public Rekognition/Azure-style cloud ToS typically restrict reverse-engineering and competitive use of services; specific 'may train on API outputs' grants are rare for FR APIs (vendor-specific ToS review required).

Risk-engineering conclusion for proprietary in-house FR: do not use InsightFace buffalo NC weights as distillation teachers in a commercial product without a paid commercial license; train on synthetic + consented data or commercially licensed teachers; treat NC-output distillation as ANECDOTAL legal grey zone with contract risk.

summary_for_decision: EU AI Act: your private photo-library person-tagger is outside Art.5 bans if you only process user-uploaded libraries and do not scrape the open web or do LE/public RBI or sensitive-attribute categorisation. Annex III high-risk RBI (1a) is the residual classification risk—Commission guidance treats media-archive FR matching as high-risk RBI; private-library tagging is not expressly exempt. If high-risk, full Chapter III duties apply from 2 Dec 2027 (post-Omnibus EC timeline); Art.50 transparency from 2 Aug 2026; prohibitions already live since 2 Feb 2025. A narrow in-house face model is almost certainly not GPAI—so no Art.53 training-data public summary. GDPR: face embeddings for unique ID are Art.9 special category → explicit consent + DPIA; account-holder ToS is not enough for third-party faces. US: BIPA §15 written release must come from photo subjects; Facebook $650M / Google $100M prove templates from user photo libraries still need subject consent; Texas CUBI similar (AG); Washington 19.375 largely carves out photo-derived data. WordPress.org: freemium SaaS OK under Guidelines 5–7 if remote service is real, documented in readme, privacy-disclosed, and local plugin is not trial-crippled; GPL applies to directory-hosted code only. Licenses: SAM1/SAM2, MobileSAM, EfficientSAM, RT-DETR, D-FINE, PP-PicoDet (via PaddleDetection) are Apache-2.0 commercial-friendly; SAM2-class is too heavy for practical ARM CPU—MobileSAM-class (~12ms class claims) or remote backend. Distillation: do not use InsightFace buffalo NC models as commercial teachers without paid license; OpenAI-style ToS bans competitive distillation from outputs; NC-output 'laundering' is ANECDOTAL grey—prefer synthetic/consented training or commercial FR licenses. Not legal advice; retain EU/US privacy counsel for Art.6 AI Act classification memo, BIPA subject-consent UX, and DPIA.
